articles.title: Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may have a reversible weakness
articles.summary: The Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may actively damage brain blood vessels and sabotage the cellular systems that remove harmful proteins. Researchers were able to reverse some of these effects in experiments, revealing promising new targets for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and other neurodegenerative diseases.
articles.content:
Mount Sinai researchers have uncovered new details about how APOE4, the strongest known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, may contribute to brain damage. Two studies published in Cell and Cell Stem Cell show that the gene can damage blood vessels in the brain and encourage the accumulation of abnormal proteins associated with neurodegenerative disease. The findings point to disease processes that may be reversible and also highlight a new human brain tissue platform derived from stem cells that could speed up the search for treatments.

Alzheimer's disease gradually damages memory, thinking, and behavior and affects more than 7 million older adults in the United States. Researchers have known for years that blood vessels in the brain deteriorate as Alzheimer's progresses, especially in people who carry APOE4. What has been less clear is why this happens and whether the vascular damage contributes directly to the disease. Because of that uncertainty, damage to the brain's circulation has often been treated as a consequence of Alzheimer's rather than as a process that could help drive it.

Mapping How APOE4 Damages Brain Blood Vessels

For the Cell study published on September 24, Mount Sinai scientists combined existing datasets to build a single cell transcriptomic atlas of blood vessels in the human brain. The resulting map showed patterns of gene activity across the different cells that create and support the brain's vascular system, giving researchers a detailed way to examine how APOE4 contributes to vascular degeneration.

The team found that APOE4 altered the behavior of pericytes. These cells normally help stabilize small blood vessels and support the blood brain barrier. In the presence of APOE4, however, the pericytes changed into myofibroblast-like cells that produce scar tissue.

That transformation promoted vascular fibrosis and increased the buildup of amyloid around blood vessels. These changes could interfere with blood flow and create conditions that encourage neurodegeneration.

The researchers also found evidence that this process could be reversed. Blocking TGF-β signaling, which plays a role in communication between cells and in tissue remodeling, restored pericyte coverage while reducing fibrosis and amyloid around blood vessels. The researchers reproduced the result in aged APOE4 mice, showing that the vascular degeneration associated with APOE4 can be therapeutically reversed.

"Damage to the brain's blood vessels is not simply a late consequence of Alzheimer's disease; it is a biologically active process caused by APOE4 that may be reversible," said corresponding author Joel W. Blanchard, PhD, Associate Professor of Neuroscience, and Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine, at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "These findings reveal new therapeutic targets for preserving vascular function and limiting amyloid accumulation."

"We show that APOE4 converts blood-vessel support cells into scar-producing cells, causing amyloid or abnormal protein buildup to accumulate around the brain's vessels. Through our experiments, we were able to block this protein buildup process, revealing possible new therapeutic treatment options and strategies for protecting the brain's circulation in people at high genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease," said first author Braxton R. Schuldt, MD/PhD candidate in Neuroscience and researcher in the Blanchard Laboratory at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai.

Human miBrains Reveal Disease Mechanisms

A major part of the research relied on miBrains, three dimensional human brain tissue developed by the Mount Sinai team from induced pluripotent stem cells. The model reproduces important features of human brain tissue, including its network of blood vessels.

The Blanchard laboratory combined findings from miBrains with preclinical models, postmortem human brain tissue, and transcriptomic data. Each approach helped confirm and expand on observations made with the others.

By bringing these systems together, the scientists were able to recreate events that occur before the severe vascular abnormalities seen in postmortem human brain tissue. They could then identify the mechanisms behind those changes and quickly test possible treatments.

APOE4 May Also Disrupt the Brain's Protein Cleanup

In the Cell Stem Cell study, researchers used miBrains to explore another effect of APOE4: its role in the accumulation of abnormal proteins associated with neurodegenerative disease.

Abnormal protein buildup is a defining feature of conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. However, investigating exactly how these deposits form inside a living human brain is extremely difficult. The miBrain system gives scientists a way to observe related processes in complex human brain-like tissue under laboratory conditions.

miBrains include all of the major cell types present in the human brain, including neurons, supporting glial cells, myelin producing cells, and cells that make up blood vessels. Similar to what happens in the human brain, miBrains carrying APOE4 developed higher amounts of abnormal alpha-synuclein. This protein is most strongly associated with Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease.

Although alpha-synuclein has major clinical importance, researchers have not fully understood the cellular processes that cause it to accumulate.

Cholesterol Buildup Disrupts Cellular Waste Removal

The experiments revealed that APOE4 causes cholesterol to accumulate inside astrocytes, support cells that perform several essential functions in maintaining brain health.

That excess cholesterol interfered with the astrocytes' lysosomal waste-disposal system. As a result, the cells became less effective at breaking down alpha-synuclein. Instead of being cleared away, the protein accumulated and spread to neurons, where it contributed to harmful deposits.

These findings suggest that cholesterol metabolism inside astrocytes, along with lysosomal function, could become important treatment targets for both Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

Using miBrains, the researchers were able to follow the chain of events in complex human brain-like tissue. Their experiments connected APOE4 with lipid buildup in astrocytes, weaker clearance of alpha-synuclein, and the formation of toxic protein deposits.

The results point to both lipid metabolism and cellular waste removal systems as potential therapeutic targets in neurodegenerative disease.

A Platform for Testing Personalized Treatments

Another advantage of the miBrain system is that researchers can preserve the tissue for future experiments.

"A key advance of our technology is that miBrains with predefined cellular compositions and disease-related factors can be cryopreserved," said Louise Mesentier-Louro, PhD, Assistant Professor of Neuroscience, and Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine, at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and first author of the Cell Stem Cell study. "This capability improves reproducibility and scalability of complex disease modeling and supports more efficient drug development and validation."

Mount Sinai researchers are also developing miBrains derived from individual patients, which could eventually allow scientists to investigate how neurodegenerative disease develops differently from person to person and how patients might respond to particular treatments.

"At Mount Sinai we are creating and cryopreserving miBrains from patients," Dr. Blanchard added. "This will enable personalized studies into how neurodegenerative disease develops and how individuals may respond to therapies. By enabling potential therapies to be tested earlier and more efficiently, the miBrain platform could help bridge the gap between laboratory discoveries and treatments for a broad range of disorders."

Study Funding

The Cell study examining vascular degeneration in the brain received support from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (80ARC022CA004), the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health (R01AG089533, UH3NS115064, U54AG090669, T32GM146636), The SWT Foundation, and the CureAlz Fund.

The Cell Stem Cell study examining abnormal protein buildup in the brain received support from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (80ARC022CA004), Aligning Science Across Parkinson's (ASAP-024297) through the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke and the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health (R01NS114239, UH3NS115064, 1U54AG090669-01, T32AG04968, F31NS13090), the CureAlz Fund, and The SWT Foundation.

The findings have broad implications for millions affected by Alzheimer's and related disorders, offering hope for future personalized therapies.

articles.title: Can pancreatic cancer be stopped in its tracks? Radical tactic raises hopes
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03119-7With prospects for new treatments at an all-time high, researchers are looking for ways to boost survival by treating the disease early.
articles.content:
Early detection of pancreatic cancer (red; artificially coloured) could help to improve the survival rates of a highly lethal disease.Credit: PDC/SPL

Armed with new tools and fresh optimism, researchers seeking to subdue pancreatic cancer — one of the world’s deadliest — are chasing a radical strategy: cancer interception.

In this approach, tissues that are growing abnormally are treated to keep them from turning cancerous and spreading. Interception is already being trialled for breast and skin cancers, among others. But now the success of a new drug that quashes pancreatic tumours is raising scientists’ hopes that interception could succeed even for this recalcitrant cancer.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

Cancer interception was one of the main themes at last week’s American Association for Cancer Research Conference (AACR) on Pancreatic Cancer in San Diego, California — the first such meeting since the US Food and Drug Administration approved the landmark pancreatic-cancer drug daraxonrasib (Rasonque) in August. Its success has renewed optimism that researchers can combine it or other emerging therapies with early-detection methods to revolutionize how pancreatic tumours are treated.

A combination of early-detection techniques and interception is “going to be the breakthrough strategy that really changes survival”, says Diane Simeone, director of the Moores Cancer Center at University of California San Diego Health. At the AACR meeting, Simeone argued that such an approach could more than triple the proportion of people who survive for five years after being diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, from 13.7% to 50%.

It’s a lofty aspiration, but other researchers are also eyeing interception. “We’re so excited that we are at this juncture now to even be considering this,” says Anirban Maitra, director of the Perlmutter Cancer Center at New York University Langone Health in New York City. “This wasn’t possible even a few years ago.”

Precautionary principle

Pancreatic tumours are notoriously wily: they are often highly invasive, impervious to most treatments and can wrap themselves around major arteries and veins, making the growths difficult to remove.

Even so, five-year survival rates can top 80% when such tumours are caught early, Simeone says. But the symptoms of pancreatic cancer are vague, and people often do not seek medical attention right away. More than half of pancreatic cancers are not diagnosed until after the disease has spread to other organs — a statistic that has remained mostly unchanged since Simeone first opened her cancer research laboratory 30 years ago.

Cancer-fighting antibodies with a one-two punch take aim at tumours

To improve early detection, she and her colleagues have launched a clinical study called PRECEDE, which aims to enrol 20,000 people who have a family history of pancreatic cancer, certain abnormal growths on their pancreas or a genetic profile that elevates their risk of the disease. The goal is to see whether — and by how much — frequent monitoring for pancreatic cancer will improve survival. So far, the team has enrolled a little more than 12,000 people, Simeone said at the conference. More than 50 participants have been diagnosed with pancreatic cancer — many of them at the earliest stages of the disease1.

The PRECEDE team plans to use samples from the study to evaluate experimental blood tests for early cancer detection, and to explore artificial-intelligence methods to detect abnormalities on the participants’ scans before they become visible to the naked eye.

In addition, Simeone says the PRECEDE consortium might test whether therapies such as daraxonrasib can boost survival rates when given immediately after surgery to remove pre-cancerous growths or early-stage tumours. Currently, daraxonrasib is only approved for advanced cancers.

Testing tolerance

Researchers at the AACR meeting heard about studies in mice that suggest the approach could work. Ben Stanger, a cancer researcher at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, and his team studied mice bearing mutations in a gene called Kras; these mutations produce proteins that can cause cancer. When the mice developed tiny, precancerous pancreatic growths, the researchers administered a drug that, like daraxonrasib, disarms KRAS and related cancer-promoting proteins. The treatment improved the animals’ survival2. “It is super exciting,” Stanger says, but adds that it could take years to determine how best to deploy the technique in people.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment through early detection and interception strategies, including a newly approved drug and ongoing large-scale clinical trials. This has the potential to greatly improve survival rates for a highly lethal cancer, impacting a broad population and offering hope for a major health challenge.

articles.title: How a simple urine test could spare most women from invasive womb cancer procedures
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at the University of Manchester developed a non-invasive womb cancer test that correctly identified most cancers and returned a negative result for 93 percent of women who did not have the disease. The test uses urine and vaginal fluid samples, is inexpensive, and requires no internal examination. In a […]
The post How a simple urine test could spare most women from invasive womb cancer procedures first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Researchers at the University of Manchester developed a non-invasive womb cancer test that correctly identified most cancers and returned a negative result for 93 percent of women who did not have the disease. The test uses urine and vaginal fluid samples, is inexpensive, and requires no internal examination.

In a study of 1,864 women with postmenopausal bleeding at seven hospitals in north-west England, 5 percent (99 women) were ultimately diagnosed with womb cancer. The test identified 80 of those 99 cases. Specialist cytologists assessed the samples blind, without knowing each woman’s diagnosis. Results were published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, and Women’s Health.

The triage gap it’s designed to close

Postmenopausal bleeding triggers an urgent cancer referral in the U.K. and in most countries. Between five and 10 percent of women referred with that symptom have womb cancer. The rest go through an internal ultrasound, a womb lining biopsy, or a hysteroscopy (a procedure in which a camera is passed into the womb), and come back clear.

“At the moment, many women face invasive, uncomfortable tests that can be stressful as well as costly for health services before cancer can be ruled out,” said Prof. Emma Davidson of the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust. The test would sort that group earlier: fast-tracking women at highest risk while giving lower-risk women a result without the camera procedure.

“Bleeding after the menopause is understandably alarming for women because it can be a sign of cancer, but the vast majority of those investigated will not have the disease,” Davidson said. “Our study shows that a simple test using urine and vaginal samples could help identify the women most likely to have cancer while safely reassuring many others much earlier in the diagnostic pathway.”

Open questions for the next phase

The samples were assessed by highly trained specialist cytologists. The researchers are upfront that they don’t know whether the same accuracy would hold in ordinary clinical settings. The test was also only studied in women who had symptoms; its performance in asymptomatic women hasn’t been established.

“If further studies confirm these findings in routine practice, this approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women every year,” Davidson said.

Hundreds of thousands of women are diagnosed with womb cancer globally each year, and many more are referred and cleared without it. If the test holds up under broader scrutiny, it would mean fewer invasive procedures for women who don’t need them, and faster answers for those who do.

Source study: The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, and Women’s Health— Urine and vaginal cytology for endometrial cancer detection in women with postmenopausal bleeding in northwest England (DETECT): diagnostic accuracy study

articles.personality_title: New urine test could reduce invasive womb cancer checks for many women

articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau test urinaire pourrait réduire les examens invasifs pour le cancer de l’utérus chez de nombreuses femmes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le cancer de l’utérus est souvent diagnostiqué grâce à des examens internes, comme des biopsies ou des caméras, qui sont inconfortables et coûteux. Beaucoup de femmes présentant des saignements après la ménopause doivent subir ces procédures pour savoir si elles ont un cancer.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Manchester ont mis au point un test simple utilisant des échantillons d’urine et de fluide vaginal pour détecter le cancer de l’utérus. Lors d’une étude menée auprès de près de 1 900 femmes saignant après la ménopause, le test a correctement détecté 80 cas sur 99 et a donné un résultat négatif pour 93 % des femmes sans cancer. Le test est peu coûteux et ne nécessite pas d’examen interne.

**Impact** – Ce test pourrait aider les médecins à identifier rapidement les femmes ayant un risque élevé de cancer de l’utérus et à rassurer en toute sécurité la majorité des autres femmes. Cela signifie que moins de femmes auraient à subir des examens invasifs et stressants, améliorant leur confort et réduisant les coûts pour la santé.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent vérifier si le test est aussi efficace dans les cliniques ordinaires et chez les femmes sans symptômes. D’autres études permettront de savoir si ce test peut devenir une méthode courante pour détecter le cancer de l’utérus.

**Une phrase clé** – Un nouveau test à base d’urine et de fluide vaginal pourrait bientôt permettre à de nombreuses femmes d’éviter des examens invasifs en identifiant avec précision qui doit faire des contrôles plus poussés.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo test de orina podría reducir exámenes invasivos para el cáncer de útero en muchas mujeres
articles.personality_presentation_es:

articles.title: Fighting dengue with sterile insects: Lisbon’s experimental approach
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Portugal has released 30,000 sterile male mosquitoes in Lisbon as part of a push to bring down populations of the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), a species that can carry dengue, Zika, and yellow fever. Last Thursday’s release in Alvalade was the third and final deployment of this phase. […]
The post Fighting dengue with sterile insects: Lisbon’s experimental approach first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Portugal has released 30,000 sterile male mosquitoes in Lisbon as part of a push to bring down populations of the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), a species that can carry dengue, Zika, and yellow fever. Last Thursday’s release in Alvalade was the third and final deployment of this phase. Sixty thousand sterile mosquitoes have now gone out across Portugal in total.

The logic behind sterile male release

Male mosquitoes don’t bite; only females do, and the sole reason they do is to get blood for egg development. Males exist to mate, which is exactly what makes this work: flood a wild population with sterile males; they compete with fertile males for females, and any female that mates with one produces nothing. Do that consistently, and reproduction rates fall. No pesticides, no genetic modification.

Afonso Moreira, a public health doctor at the Francisco George Public Health Unit and the project’s lead researcher, says the sterilization method is proven and safe. Sterile insect technique has a long track record in agricultural pest control. Its use against disease-carrying mosquitoes in European cities is a newer application.

Dispersal and survival: the first phase focus

Bringing down the population isn’t the immediate goal. Researchers are working through a more basic question first: how far do the released mosquitoes spread, and how long do they last once they’re out in a city?

“When we release them into areas where there is a population of this mosquito, they will essentially compete with the male mosquitoes that are already there, the wild mosquitoes,” Moreira told the Lusa news agency.

If the dispersal and survival numbers hold up, the next stage will be a comparative study starting in May, measuring reproduction in treated areas against areas handled through conventional methods.

One piece of a broader strategy

Moreira was clear that sterile releases aren’t a replacement for anything. Getting rid of standing water and cutting off breeding sites is still the most direct way to keep tiger mosquito numbers in check. The sterile male program adds pressure from inside the population, but the habitat work has to keep running alongside it.

The disease risk from Aedes albopictus works through a chain: the mosquito picks up a pathogen from an infected person and passes it to whoever it bites next. Fewer mosquitoes mean fewer chances for that chain to close.

articles.personality_title: Lisbon tests sterile mosquitoes to reduce disease-carrying pests
articles.personality_presentation:

This was the third and final release in the current phase, adding up to 60,000 sterile mosquitoes released across the country. Male mosquitoes don’t bite, but they compete with wild males to mate with females. Since these released males are sterile, females that mate with them lay eggs that don’t hatch.

**Impact** – This method lowers mosquito numbers without using pesticides or changing mosquito genes. It is safer and more environmentally friendly than spraying chemicals. The project’s first goal was to see how far the sterile mosquitoes travel and how long they survive in the city. If successful, it will help reduce disease risks by lowering mosquito populations.

**What's next step** – Starting in May, researchers will compare areas with sterile mosquito releases to areas treated with usual methods. They want to see which approach works better to stop mosquitoes from reproducing. Meanwhile, people will still need to remove standing water where mosquitoes breed to support this effort.

articles.personality_title_fr: Lisbonne teste des moustiques stériles pour réduire les nuisibles porteurs de maladies
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Lisbonne doit faire face au moustique tigre asiatique, qui peut transmettre des maladies comme la dengue, le Zika et la fièvre jaune. Ces moustiques sont un problème de santé dans de nombreuses villes car ils piquent les humains et peuvent transmettre des infections.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le Portugal a lâché 30 000 moustiques mâles stériles tigres asiatiques dans le quartier d’Alvalade à Lisbonne. C’était la troisième et dernière phase de cette étape, totalisant 60 000 moustiques stériles lâchés dans tout le pays. Les moustiques mâles ne piquent pas, mais ils rivalisent avec les mâles sauvages pour s’accoupler avec les femelles. Comme ces mâles sont stériles, les femelles pondent des œufs qui ne vont pas éclore.

**Impact** – Cette méthode réduit le nombre de moustiques sans utiliser de pesticides ni modifier leurs gènes. C’est plus sûr et meilleur pour l’environnement que les traitements chimiques. Le but premier était d’observer jusqu’où les moustiques stériles se déplacent et combien de temps ils survivent en ville. Si cela fonctionne, cela aidera à réduire les risques de maladies en diminuant la population de moustiques.

**Prochaine étape** – À partir de mai, les chercheurs compareront des zones avec lâchers de moustiques stériles à des zones traitées par les méthodes habituelles. Ils veulent voir quelle méthode est la plus efficace pour empêcher la reproduction des moustiques. En même temps, il faut continuer à éliminer l’eau stagnante où les moustiques se reproduisent.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le lâcher de moustiques mâles stériles à Lisbonne offre une nouvelle méthode sûre pour réduire les moustiques porteurs de maladies en bloquant leur reproduction.
articles.personality_title_es: Lisboa prueba mosquitos estériles para reducir plagas que transmiten enfermedades
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Lisboa enfrenta un problema con el mosquito tigre asiático, que puede transmitir enfermedades como el dengue, Zika y la fiebre amarilla. Estos mosquitos son un problema de salud en muchas ciudades porque pican a las personas y pueden pasar infecciones.

**Qué pasó** – Portugal liberó 30,000 mosquitos machos estériles tigre asiáticos en el barrio de Alvalade en Lisboa. Esta fue la tercera y última liberación de esta fase, sumando un total de 60,000 mosquitos estériles liberados en todo el país. Los mosquitos machos no pican, pero compiten con los machos salvajes para aparearse con las hembras. Como estos machos están estériles, las hembras ponen huevos que no nacen.

**Impacto** – Este método reduce el número de mosquitos sin usar pesticidas ni modificar sus genes. Es más seguro y mejor para el ambiente que los químicos. El primer objetivo fue ver qué tan lejos se dispersan los mosquitos estériles y cuánto tiempo sobreviven en la ciudad. Si funciona, ayudará a bajar el riesgo de enfermedades al reducir la población de mosquitos.

Quieren ver qué método es mejor para detener la reproducción de mosquitos. Mientras tanto, es importante seguir eliminando el agua estancada donde se reproducen.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La liberación de mosquitos machos estériles en Lisboa es una forma nueva y segura de reducir los mosquitos que transmiten enfermedades al impedir que se reproduzcan.
